cards.q: What three parts must a measurable question name?
cards.a: A metric (a number computed in a defined way), a slice (period, city, segment) and a comparison (against what). Example: churn share of Q3 customers, Student versus Regular.

cards.q: ShopKart's late rate is 13.8% with the right denominator but 11.8% with all orders. Which denominator is right and why?
cards.a: Orders that have both a promised and an actual delivery time (17,208). Store pickups and cancellations have no delivery time, so they cannot be late, and counting them in the denominator pushes the rate down.

cards.q: What does it mean for a data load to be idempotent, and how do you get it?
cards.a: Running it twice leaves the same table as running it once. Give the table a primary key and load with an upsert (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT(order_id) DO UPDATE), not a plain append.

cards.q: Why can a watermark load (WHERE order_date > last loaded date) lose data?
cards.a: Late-arriving rows (dated 30 June, arriving 2 July) are skipped, and later updates to old rows (delivered becomes returned) are never seen. Safer: reload a sliding window of N days with an upsert, N longer than the longest delay.

cards.q: Why is drop_duplicates(subset=['customer_id','product']) a wrong dedupe for an orders table?
cards.a: Customers legitimately buy the same product more than once, so it deletes real orders and shrinks revenue. Drop on the full row, or on the true key (order_id) after checking that duplicated ids carry identical values.

cards.q: Why should missing delivery_minutes on cancelled orders not be filled with 0?
cards.a: The value is not applicable, it is not zero. About 2,800 fake zeros would drag the average delivery time down. Leave it missing so averages skip it, and compute the late rate only over orders with both times.

cards.q: Quartiles are 30 and 45 minutes. What are the 1.5 x IQR fences, and who decides what is an error?
cards.a: IQR = 15, so lower = 30 - 22.5 = 7.5 and upper = 45 + 22.5 = 67.5. Statistics only find suspects. A domain rule (for example 5 to 300 minutes) decides which suspects are errors and which are real extremes.

cards.q: What is the join fan-out trap and how do you catch it?
cards.a: If the right table has several rows per key, each left row repeats and sums inflate (revenue doubled with two campaigns per category). Compare row counts before and after, and use merge(validate='m:1') or HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.

cards.q: Why is the mean of city average order values wrong for the overall average, and what is right?
cards.a: It gives small cities the same weight as big ones. Use total revenue divided by total orders (a weighted mean). Averages of 800, 900, 1,000 and 1,100 on 10, 10, 10 and 970 orders give 1,094, not 950.

cards.q: Why must a monthly running total be computed in a CTE before you filter to a few months?
cards.a: SQL applies WHERE before window functions in the same query, so filtering first makes the running total cover only the kept months. Compute SUM() OVER (ORDER BY month) in the CTE, then filter outside it.

cards.q: What does a 95% confidence interval for the mean delivery time describe, and what does it not describe?
cards.a: Plausible values for the long-run mean (40.1 to 40.4 minutes here). It is not the range holding 95% of deliveries: individual times vary with a standard deviation near 9 minutes.

cards.q: If you check an A/A test 20 times and stop at the first p < 0.05, how often do you declare a false win?
cards.a: About 23.5% in the chapter's simulation (2,000 runs, 500 users per look), not 5%. Fix the sample size in advance and look once, or use a sequential method built for repeated looks.

cards.q: Why score a forecast over several rolling origins instead of one hold-out?
cards.a: One hold-out can mislead. On the last 28 days the naive forecast won (MAE 9.8), but averaged over five origins the 7-day moving average was best (9.4 against 10.9 for naive).

cards.q: What should an AUC of 0.99 or 1.0 make you suspect first, and what is the check?
cards.a: Leakage. Ask of each feature whether it is known at prediction time. Adding delivery_minutes (it defines the target) lifted AUC from 0.836 to 1.0. Rerun with a time split; if the score collapses, you found leakage, not a model.

cards.q: Name four kinds of leakage, with one example each from the delivery data.
cards.a: Target (delivery_minutes as a feature), preprocessing (scaler fitted before the split), temporal (random split of time-ordered orders), group or history (customer lateness averaged over all orders, including the one being predicted).

cards.q: A flag costs 5, a flagged late order costs 20 more, a missed late order costs 60. At what probability is flagging worth it?
cards.a: Act when P x (60 - 20) > 5, so P > 5/40 = 0.125, if probabilities are calibrated. The empirical best threshold on validation data was 0.11, close to the theory.

cards.q: Why does TF-IDF search fail for 'something to keep my phone charged' when the product is a Power Bank?
cards.a: They share no words, and TF-IDF measures word overlap only. Embeddings place related meanings close together. Measure retrieval on a labelled query set before connecting an LLM.

cards.q: Which three instructions in a RAG prompt reduce hallucination?
cards.a: Answer only from the passages, say 'I do not know' if the answer is absent, and cite passage numbers so a human can check. Also measure retrieval separately from answer faithfulness.

cards.q: Why must you save the preprocessing together with the model?
cards.a: Predictions depend on the exact encoders and scalers used in training. Rebuilding them by hand (categories in another order) silently gives garbage: training-serving skew. Save one pipeline and test the reloaded copy on golden inputs.

cards.q: Give the PSI formula and the usual rule-of-thumb levels.
cards.a: PSI = sum over bins of (b - a) x ln(b/a), with a the reference share and b the new share. Below 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 watch, above 0.25 shift. These cut-offs are conventions, not laws.

quiz.q: In ShopKart, 17,208 cleaned orders have both a promised and an actual delivery time, and 2,367 of them are late. The cleaned file has 19,995 orders. Which late rate should the dashboard show?
opts: 86.2%, the on-time share
14.8%, returned orders divided by all orders
quiz.why: Lateness exists only where both times exist, so the denominator is 17,208. The tempting 11.8% divides by all orders and counts store pickups and cancellations as on time, which hides late deliveries.

quiz.q: A nightly load uses WHERE order_date > :watermark. An order dated 30 June reaches the source on 2 July, after the watermark moved to 1 July. What happens?
opts: It is loaded twice
The job stops with a unique-key error
It is loaded and an older row is overwritten
It is skipped and never loaded
quiz.why: The filter looks only at dates after the watermark, so a late-arriving row dated before it is missed for good. A sliding-window reload with an upsert catches it. Duplicates or key errors would need the row to be selected first.

quiz.q: What does Python print for sorted(['10', '9', '100'])?
quiz.why: Strings sort character by character: '1' comes before '9', and '10' comes before '100' because a prefix sorts first. The numeric order [9, 10, 100] appears only after converting to numbers, which is why types must be fixed early.

quiz.q: Orders are merged on category with a table that has two rows per category. What does the merged frame show?
opts: The same rows and unchanged revenue
Twice as many rows but unchanged revenue
Twice as many rows and revenue doubled
The same rows but revenue doubled
quiz.why: Each order matches two promo rows, so rows double and a sum over the merged revenue column doubles too. The tempting 'same rows' answer forgets that a many-to-many match repeats left rows. Check validate='m:1' or the row counts.

quiz.q: A Power BI measure using SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR returns blanks. Which check comes first?
opts: That the fact table has two years of data in a text column
Rewrite the measure with SUM instead of CALCULATE
That a complete date table exists, is related to the fact table, and the measure uses its Date column
Set the relationship to both directions
quiz.why: Time intelligence needs a date table with every date and a relationship to the facts, and the function must use that table's Date column, not the fact table's date. Changing the aggregation or the filter direction does not supply the missing calendar.

quiz.q: 130 of 1,000 App orders and 150 of 1,000 Web orders are late. What does the pooled two-proportion z-test say?
opts: z is about 1.29, p about 0.20: not significant at 5%
z is about 2.58, p about 0.01: significant
z is about 0.64, p about 0.52: not significant
z is about 1.82, p about 0.07: not significant
quiz.why: Pooled rate 0.14, standard error sqrt(0.14 x 0.86 x 2/1000) = 0.0155, z = 0.02 / 0.0155 = 1.29. Using the single-group standard error (0.0110) gives the tempting 1.82. The same 2-point gap becomes significant only with much more data.

quiz.q: The Web versus App late-rate gap has p = 0.0006 and survives stratifying by promise length. Which statement is best supported?
opts: Web causes lateness, so promote the App
There is a 0.06% chance that the channels are really the same
The gap is large, because p is small
The gap is unlikely to be chance and survives one confounder check; its cause is still open, and an experiment would settle it
quiz.why: A small p-value says the gap is unlikely to be chance, not why it exists, nor that it is large. Passing one adjustment does not rule out other confounders (city, hour, basket), so a randomised test is the way to decide.

quiz.q: You predict lateness at the moment an order is placed. Which column is a legitimate feature?
opts: delivery_minutes
promised_minutes
status
revenue
quiz.why: The promise is set at order time. delivery_minutes defines the target, and status and revenue are only known after delivery, so each would leak the answer (AUC 1.0). Always ask what you would know at prediction time.

quiz.q: A flag costs 5, a flagged late order costs 20 more, and a missed late order costs 60. An order has a calibrated P(late) = 0.12. What do you do?
opts: Do not flag: acting costs 5 + 20 x 0.12 = 7.4, not acting costs 60 x 0.12 = 7.2
Flag it: 5 is far below 60, so always act
Flag it: 0.12 is close to the 0.14 base rate
Flag it only if the model's AUC is above 0.8
quiz.why: Break-even is P = 5/40 = 0.125, so 0.12 is just below it. The tempting answer compares 5 with 60, but a miss only costs 40 more than a flagged late order, and most flags hit orders that were never late.

quiz.q: scikit-learn's smoothed idf is ln((1 + N)/(1 + df)) + 1. For a word in 2 of 3 documents, what is it?
quiz.why: ln(4/3) + 1 = 1.2877. The tempting 1.4055 is ln(3/2) + 1, the unsmoothed form; 0.4055 forgets the +1; 1.5 is just N/df. The hand calculation matches scikit-learn's TfidfVectorizer.

quiz.q: A feature has reference shares 50/30/20 and new shares 40/30/30 over three bins. What is the PSI and the verdict?
opts: 0.063: stable (below 0.1)
0.300: shift (above 0.25)
quiz.why: PSI = (0.4-0.5) ln(0.8) + 0 + (0.3-0.2) ln(1.5) = 0.0223 + 0.0405 = 0.063. Summing the log ratios without the (b - a) weights gives the tempting 0.182, and summing the absolute gaps gives 0.20.

quiz.q: A key feature's PSI jumps to 0.4, but AUC on newly labelled data is unchanged. What is the best response?
opts: Ignore it, because AUC is unchanged
Retrain immediately, because PSI above 0.25 requires it
Roll back to the previous model version
Investigate the cause (new city, data bug, upstream change) and check performance sooner; the model may still be fine
quiz.why: Input drift is an early warning and needs labels to confirm harm. Ignoring it risks a later surprise; retraining blindly may bake in a data bug. Find the cause first and bring the next performance check forward.
